# 10-palus: sources

Back-test entry `10-palus.yaml`: Palus Finance, more yield on a startup's idle cash (YC Winter 2026). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only. Quotes are verbatim. **[author]** marks a choice the public material does not make, kept as small as it could be.

Sources, with the short names used below:
- **HN**: Launch HN, 2026-03-06, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47278980 (the founders' post and 89 comments). A comment is cited as HN/NNN, meaning https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=NNN.
- **YCL**: Launch YC post, https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/PfC-palus-finance-better-yields-on-idle-cash-for-startups-and-smbs
- **YCC**: YC company page, https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/palus-finance
- **SITE**: https://palus.finance and https://www.palus.finance/treasury (read 2026-10-22)

Status today: same customer, a wider offer. The YC page says "Palus is your startup's financial advisor". The homepage now says "The world's most advanced fractional CFO firm" (SITE). The treasury product is still on /treasury.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (actor, segment, roles).** The founder was his own customer:
- "we realized we needed the product for our own startup’s cash reserves, and other startups in the batch started telling us they wanted this too" (HN).
- The co-founder named who it is for: "this product is for startups and SMBs that don't have the time or resources to host a fractional CFO or a full-time finance team" (HN/47283812).
- A sceptic named the two people whose time it costs: "the founder, or an ops person's time" (HN/47297953).
- *Roles.* Keel's B2B shape needs one role that lives the problem and another that decides to buy. At a funded startup the person who moves the cash every month is the one who runs finance day to day (a finance or ops lead, or a fractional CFO). The person who signs where the reserve sits is the founder-CEO. The founders aim their product and copy at founders: "We optimized our UX for founders" (HN/47290652). So `finance_lead` is the practitioner (12 people, Parts 1 and 2) and `founder` is the decision-maker (8 people, Part 3). The same company pays.
- **[author]** The split is mine. At the smallest startups the two roles are one person. That is why one practitioner (Grace Mbeki) passes the job to a fractional CFO, and why the commercial vector is read from founders.
- *Segment*: "Startups and SMBs" banking with "Brex, Mercury, etc." (HN). **[author]** I narrowed it to US venture-backed startups within two years of a raise, to match the occasion the founder describes.

**2. What (the job).** The job is to earn more on the cash without risking it and without switching banks:
- "earn higher yields with a high-yield bond portfolio" (HN).
- "a way to earn more yield on fundraise proceeds without switching banks" (YCC, as summarised from the page).
- Context job **[author]**, worded from these: "keep the money from a raise safe and earning until the company spends it".

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- "The typical startup cashflow pattern is a large infusion from a raise covering 18–24 months of burn, drawn down gradually" (HN).
- "you’re giving up yield to get same-day liquidity on cash you won’t touch for six months or more" (HN).
- The repeated moment is the monthly transfer: "easy to set up rules like ("if my bank balance falls below $X then transfer $Y from treasury")" (HN/47280293).
- **[author]** The occasion "cash decision", the window {3, MONTHS}, Frequency 2 to 3 months out of 3, and Prevalence "Most" (p_60_80) are mine. They follow from "drawn down gradually" (a monthly move), and they match 05-paidly's three-month window.

**4. Which people (comparable group).**
- "Say you (like many startups) use Mercury Treasury, Rho Treasury, Brex Treasury, etc." (HN/47280293).
- "founders who've thought about idle cash management" (HN).
- **[author]** The Importance rivals come from what the thread itself raises:
  - runway: "an extra month or two of runway", HN/47282750
  - safety above the insured limit: the SVB-style worry in HN/47279304 and HN/47279349
  - getting cash back fast: "1-2 business days", HN
  - moving money without mistakes: "no manual reconciliation between accounts", HN/47283812

**5. Who pays.**
- The company pays a fee on its own balance: "We will charge a flat 0.25% annual fee on AUM" (HN).
- The founder decides. The pitch is to the founder's time: "It's a one-time setup that takes five minutes. We optimized our UX for founders" (HN/47290652).
- Buyer and payer:
  - **[author]** The founder's tested item is "Nobody else", which fits the five-minute pitch.
  - "The board" is the one other role on the founder's list. The thread itself puts it there: "I am not sure I would suggest my portfolio companies to risk their treasuries" (HN/47279377). SITE also says the design follows "NVCA startup treasury guidelines".
- Purchase friction:
  - "Diligence on a new provider" comes from "it definitely takes weeks to diligence your company and the offering" (HN/47401784).
  - "A tax adviser's sign-off" comes from "they should talk to their tax advisor" (HN/47282781).
  - "Board approval of the cash policy" **[author]**.

**6. Mechanism.**
- "we built Palus to connect to your existing bank account via Plaid" (HN).
- "Our bond portfolio holds short-duration floating-rate" government-backed mortgage-backed securities, "managed by Regan Capital, which runs MBSF" (HN).
- "Liquidity is typically available in 1-2 business days" (HN).
- "All assets are held with an SEC-licensed custodian" (HN).
- "two buttons and a giant number that goes up" (HN).
- Compatibility conditions, Adoption friction efforts and the Commitment step:
  - The tested condition, "They could wait two days for their cash", is the founder's own claim: "most startups can afford to take on a bit more liquidity risk on their long-term cash (on the order of a couple of days)" (HN/47282907).
  - The commitment step comes from "I'd encourage you to start small, try us out, and grow your position over time" (HN/47280532).
  - The tested effort, "Move the long-term reserve out of the bank's treasury", **[author]**, worded from "The problem is the treasury product bundled with them, not the bank" (HN).

**7. Price.**
- "We will charge a flat 0.25% annual fee on AUM, compared to the 0.15–0.60%, depending on balance, charged by other treasury providers" (HN).
- "Rho charges a variable rate that peaks at 0.6% for any deposit of $2M or less" (HN/47280707).
- Yields: "we target 4.5–5% returns vs. roughly 3.5% from most money market funds" (HN). SITE now says "targeted SOFR + 1% spread".
- **[author]** Keel's price is a money range over a period, and its ladder stops below $10,000. So I state the fee per month on the reserve the founder's own example uses, $4M to $6M: 0.25% of that is $10,000 to $15,000 a year, so $800 to $1,200 a month.
- **[author]** The cost estimate, $4,000 to $6,000 a month, is the yield given up. The founder says "on $5M, it's an extra $50k-75k per year" (HN/47280107), which is about $4,200 to $6,250 a month, rounded to the range. It counts yield given up, which the registry's meaning allows ("foregone alternatives"). It does not count the 0.15% to 0.60% fee the bank's product already takes.
- **[author]** The hourly rate, $75, is mine: a startup finance lead's salary of about $150k a year, over a working year.
- Ability to pay is derived by code: 13% to 30%, small_share.

**8. Occasions (real accounts).**
- No named customer quote is public. HN is the record: batchmates "started telling us they wanted this too" (HN), one sign-up, "I’ve wanted this produce for years. Signed up." (HN/47283895), and many sceptics. Each respondent below is traced to one of them.

## Respondents

Practitioners (primary link, `finance_lead`):
- Dana Whitfield: HN/47279411 ("we wouldn't want to switch even for a higher yield… the operational burden is more important to us than yield", "about 3.2%"). The $300k transfer is **[author]**.
- Marcus Oyelaran: HN/47279219 (self-directed brokerage, "more paperwork and back and forth", then "click that button now!"). The $3M and August are **[author]**.
- Lena Hofstra: HN/47279349 ("nowhere near juicy enough for me to literally bet the company on") and HN/47279304 (bank-run worry). The Treasuries-only policy and the two banks are **[author]**, after the 2023 bank failures the thread refers to.
- Tomás Reyes: HN/47283895 ("I’ve wanted this produce for years"), with the launch post's "large infusion from a raise". Cash sitting in plain checking is **[author]**.
- Aisha Karimi: HN/47279292 ("business savings accounts not much below this (2.85%) while keeping things safe (FDIC insured)").
- Ben Okafor: HN/47280707 (the fee "peaks at 0.6% for any deposit of $2M or less"). The $1.5M is **[author]**.
- Rachel Lindqvist: HN/47282512 and HN/47283590 (PHC and QSBS: "a bunch of startups are raising $20m on $0 revenue … interest … can easily be the only income").
- Hiro Tanabe (gate No): HN/47279242 ("Startups otherwise are lean and won't hold enough cash to get a meaningful return").
- Grace Mbeki: HN/47283265 ("they might be better suited to deal with a fractional CFO service"). The Slack approval is **[author]**; the YC page (YCC) says the firm is reachable around the clock on Slack (paraphrased).
- Owen Castellano (chip): author's invention, filling a gap: no commenter refuses to say. A chipped story is needed so the reading counts one GUESSED person. It loosely echoes HN/47279377 (an investor steering portfolio companies).
- Nadia Seferović: HN/47286820 ("ask your bank manager for rates on a 30 day deposit account … it appeared in my online banking the next day").
- Kevin Duarte: the launch post ("a mutual fund where your principal is at considerable risk – it had a 9% loss in 2022") and HN/47280944 (the short-term bond fund in "one of the leading startup treasury products"). Moving the loss to August 2026 is **[author]**.

Decision-makers (`link: COMMERCIAL_B2B`, `founder`, Part 3 only, no story on screen):
- Sofia Marchetti: author's invention, filling a gap: the thread has almost no willing buyer. She stands for the founders' own case ("putting $5M into Palus yields them an extra $50k-75k per year", HN/47290584) and the batchmates who "wanted this too" (HN). Her $2,000 a month is the bank's treasury fee.
- Jamal Booker: HN/47297953 ("That 50-75k is more like $5k/month out of what is typically a ~200-400k monthly burn") and HN/47401784 ("it definitely takes weeks to diligence").
- Eleanor Vance: HN/47279349 ("bet the company"); the board having to agree is **[author]**.
- Ravi Menon: HN/47279377 ("I am not sure I would suggest my portfolio companies to risk their treasuries"). The investor who had to agree is his.
- Maya Feldman: HN/47283895 (signed up) and HN/47283356 (liked "a number that goes up").
- Daniel Osei: HN/47283590 ("The probability is Low but the impact for us is massive"). The tax adviser's long sign-off is his.
- Irene Kowal: HN/47279831 ("This should be a hard pass for literally everyone … SGOV") and HN/47279261 ("just put the money in a Bond ETF").
- Felix Brandt: HN/47282750 ("I am willing to take a little bit more risk for a higher return … an extra month or two of runway").

No respondent carries a commenter's handle or a real customer's name (SITE names client companies; none is used).

## Open

- **Relative advantage code.** The registry fixes five advantage codes (fewer_attempts, shorter_time, less_worry, less_help_needed, easier_recovery). None means "more money". I used `less_help_needed` with the founder's label "Higher yield without hiring for treasury". It is the closest code, and it carries the founder's claim of "no need to hire for treasury operations" (HN/47283812). A yield code would fit better.
- **Price period.** Palus prices a share of the balance, not an amount per period. The $800 to $1,200 a month depends on the $4M to $6M reserve I chose. Keel has no "percent of balance" price.
- **Cost estimate kind.** The founder's cost is yield given up, not money spent. Decision-makers asked "what it cost the team last month" will report fees and hours, so Existing sacrifice is likely to read far below the founder's estimate. That is a real finding about this idea, but it is also partly an artefact of the question's wording.
- **Window.** The {3, MONTHS} window and the "cash decision" occasion are mine. Public material has no single trigger moment, only "drawn down gradually".
- **Not checked against the engine.** The file passes keel-e2e-eval's `instructions/corpus.py` loader (bound to the registry) and every rule of `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` but S/C/V. Those three need the `expected` block, which a back-test omits by design.

insights.line: What would have made a difference

whys.g1: Getting cash out in time and keeping it insured are two concerns I'd recognise as different, both names are plain, and Marcus's point about separate paperwork and transfers doesn't really fit either group, so leaving it on its own is fair.
whys.g2: There is no junk on this line; all five answers are real replies about what would have made a difference.

whys.g1: Rachel's answer is about runway and her accountant wanting plain cash for tax, not about pulling cash out when bills are due, so it sits oddly in 'Getting cash out when it's needed'; the other placements and both names are ones I'd recognise, and Aisha's insured-and-explainable answer rightly stands alone.
whys.g2: There is no junk, explicit or off-topic answer on this line; all six are real answers about why moving the cash felt like too much.

founder.order_why: The flow runs context, problem, solution and pilot in a sensible order, but screens 20 and 21 are headed INTERVIEWS · SENT while still asking how people should answer and who gets a link, so the study reads as sent before I've chosen who receives it.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 4 show the identical question ('Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies.'), and screen 9 asks for a name again after screen 1 named the project; for me both names are 'Palus'.
founder.missing: Relative advantage (13-14) has no 'what do you believe is true?' screen, unlike compatibility (12) and adoption friction (17), so the claim I most want tested goes unasked: more yield (4.5-5% against about 3.5%) without switching banks. Nothing asks whether a finance lead trusts a non-bank with the reserve (principal risk, SEC custodian, the 2022 bond-fund loss), which is the main objection in my launch thread.

PRIMARY.order_why: The 'could you have waited two days to get your cash back' question comes before I'm asked whether Palus would have helped, so it reads like a product constraint quizzed on me before I've weighed the idea, and it would sit more naturally after the 'better or not' question alongside the moving-the-reserve question.
PRIMARY.missing: Nobody asked where our cash actually sits today (Mercury/Brex treasury, sweep, T-bills), what yield we get on it, or how much operational burden we'd accept to switch — for me the hassle of moving and managing money matters more than a higher yield, and the study never asked how we weigh safety, yield and effort, or who else (CEO, board) has a say in where the cash sits.

screens.why3: A finance lead knows where the reserve sat at their last cash decision and whether it earned more or needed less of their time, and I know my own claim.
screens.why4: The two rows are distinct and mine, 'higher yield than where the cash sits today' and 'no treasury hire', and nothing I claimed is missing, since 'without switching banks' was already covered as fit.
screens.why5: My claim is more yield on the reserve without hiring for treasury, and the generic 'better' blurs that, while 'last cash decision' leans on the monthly transfer more than where the long-term reserve sits.
screens.instead: For most, the cash from their raise would have earned more at their last cash decision, without anyone hired to manage it. Rows: Higher yield than where the cash sits today / No treasury hire needed to manage the cash.

screens.why1: After fit and advantage, asking what a finance lead must do to start is the natural last solution question, and it's where my Plaid link and the reserve move belong.
screens.why2: 'Setup, extra steps or learning' is plain to me, and 'bank's treasury' and 'long-term reserve' are my trade's words.
screens.why3: I built the onboarding myself, so I know exactly what a finance lead has to do: connect the account and move the reserve.
screens.why4: The only option is the escape chip, 'Leave this out of the study', which fits a free-text answer that a founder might not want tested.
screens.why5: Keel kept my reserve move word for word but dropped the Plaid link, and 'Most would move…' turns a step they must take into a guess about how many would do it, which drifts a little from what I typed.
screens.instead: What will they have to do to start using it? (keep the box) -- and have Keel write: 'To start, they would link the company bank account through Plaid and move the long-term reserve out of the bank's treasury.'

screens.why1: Right after I said what they would have to do to start, Keel shows back the efforts it drew and which one it will test, so it is obvious why this check sits here.
screens.why2: Plaid, long-term reserve and the bank's treasury are everyday words to me and to a startup finance lead on Mercury or Brex, so I read it once.
screens.why3: These are the two moves I am asking my own customers to make, and I know exactly what each one costs a finance lead.
screens.why4: The two rows are distinct and in my words, but the step that takes the real time is missing: opening the account with the custodian and passing its onboarding and KYC, which is the 'weeks to diligence' the thread complains about.
screens.why5: The tested effort is the one I chose, moving the reserve out of the bank's treasury rather than switching banks, and the belief keeps that meaning.
screens.instead: Rows: Link the company bank account through Plaid / Open the custodian account and pass its onboarding / Move the long-term reserve out of the bank's treasury; belief unchanged.

screens.why1: Right after I listed the two steps a customer must take to start, it is obvious why Keel asks which of them the study should test, as the last of the four solution beliefs.
screens.why2: 'Long-term reserve', 'the bank's treasury' and 'link through Plaid' are my own words and how a startup finance person talks about Mercury or Brex Treasury, so I read it once and know what it means.
screens.why3: I know my onboarding: Plaid linking is a five-minute click, and the real hurdle is getting the reserve out of the bank's bundled treasury, so I can pick from what I know.
screens.why4: These are exactly the two efforts I typed, they are distinct, and the second is clearly the one worth testing, so nothing is missing or doubled.
screens.why5: The belief 'Most would move the long-term reserve out of the bank's treasury', with the one-in-three bar, is the step I named and the bet my product rests on, unchanged.

screens.why1: After the solution beliefs are chosen, a pilot screen before strangers see it is the obvious next step in step 4.
screens.why2: "The pilot" as a bare heading doesn't tell me what the pilot is (how many people, which link, what I get), and "locking freezes your beliefs" needs a second read to see it is irreversible.
screens.why3: Whether I'm ready to lock what I believe and send it is entirely my own call as the founder.
screens.why4: The only choice is "Continue"; there is no visible way to go back and edit a belief or to see the questions before locking, so a founder who wants to check is left without an option.
screens.why5: Nothing of my idea is reworded here; it only freezes what I typed.
screens.instead: Ready to send a small pilot? Locking freezes your beliefs (compatibility: they could wait two days for their cash; effort: move the long-term reserve out of the bank's treasury) and writes the questions finance leads and founders will see -- [Lock and preview the questions] [Go back and edit]

screens.why1: Choosing who runs the interviews belongs right before the study goes out, after the pilot, so the reason it is asked is obvious.
screens.why2: "Who asks the questions" is plain, but "Keel's credits", "the face Keel preselects" and "lock and record the interviewer" are tool jargon I would need to read twice, not words from my trade.
screens.why3: Whether I want an AI interviewer or a text link sent to finance leads is my own call about my own study.
screens.why4: The choice seems to be the AI interviewer (with a preselected face) or text links, which covers it, but "lock and record" blurs whether I am picking a face, a mode, or both.
screens.why5: Nothing about Palus, the finance leads or the founders is touched here, so my words are kept and none leak to a respondent.
screens.instead: Who should ask your finance leads the questions? — An AI interviewer by voice (uses Keel credits) / A written link they fill in themselves

screens.why1: Choosing how strangers answer belongs right before sending, after the pilot and who asks the questions are settled.
screens.why2: "Text only" and "Let them choose" read at once, but the AI interviewer line is muddled: "Every answer in a quiet room. More than 90% in loud places down to 5 dB.Hear it" runs a claim into a button label, and 5 dB is near silence, not a loud place, so I had to read it twice and still can't tell what it promises.
screens.why3: I know my finance leads sit at desks and would rather read and tap than talk to a video face about where our cash sits, so I can answer this from what I know of them.
screens.why4: The three choices are complete and distinct and "Text only" is there for me, but the AI option's accuracy claim is garbled and "needs Keel's credits" is pasted onto the descriptions instead of sitting apart as a note.
screens.why5: My pick of "Text only" is shown as I made it, and nothing of Palus or the finance-lead and founder roles leaks into this screen.
screens.instead: How should they answer? — AI interviewer: a face on video asks each question aloud; they answer by talking or tapping (catches over 90% of spoken answers, even in noisy places; uses Keel credits) · Text only: they read each question and tap · Let them choose: both offered, they pick when they open the link (uses Keel credits)

screens.why1: A first-screen check that my company is US-based and recently raised is exactly where a study about where raise cash sits should start, though the kicker's 'A recent time' does not match a who-are-you question.
screens.why2: 'A raise' is plain to me, but the question joins two conditions with 'and', so I have to check both before I can say yes; it is answerable, but it is double-barrelled.
screens.why3: I know where we are based and when we closed our round without thinking about it.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, since if either part fails the answer is No, and a gate needs no escape.
screens.why5: It keeps the US and the two-year window but drops venture-backed and the Mercury or Brex style of banking, so it lets in companies the founder did not mean.
screens.why6: It is short and the two options are easy to hold, but a listener has to carry two conditions in one breath before answering.
screens.instead: Did your company close a venture round in the last two years? Yes; or No. (with 'Is the company based in the US?' asked as its own gate first)

screens.why1: A gate on whether our raise was sitting around makes sense after the US-and-raise gate, but the follow-up asks for my last cash decision, so the gate doesn't line up with the story it opens.
screens.why2: "Sit idle" needs a second read: our cash is never idle in my head, it sits in a Mercury treasury sweep at about 3.2%, so I don't know if that counts as idle or not.
screens.why3: I know exactly where our raised cash has been these last three months, I run those accounts.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it, but there are two escape chips where there should be one, and "I'd rather not say" is one the guidelines rule out, while "I can't recall one particular cash decision" answers a different question than idle cash.
screens.why5: "Idle" carries the founder's pitch that money is leaking yield, which I'd push back on; for us the operational burden matters more than yield, so the word leans the question toward their product.
screens.why6: Short and said as "Yes or no", but the spoken form drops the escape altogether, and on screen there are two chips, one of them a mouthful.
screens.instead: In the last 3 months, did you decide where some of the company's raised cash should sit, or not? Yes / No; escape: I can't recall

screens.why1: Right after asking whether our raised cash sat idle, showing an idea for putting that idle cash to work is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: I'd say floating-rate Treasuries or T-bills, so 'government-backed bonds with interest that adjusts' takes me a second read to work out what they actually buy, and 'government-backed' could mean agencies, not Treasuries.
screens.why3: Where our reserve sits, what it earns, how fast it comes back to checking and who holds it are exactly the things I weigh day to day.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options shown.
screens.why5: Nothing leaks, but 'government-backed bonds with interest that adjusts' reads like a paraphrase of something more precise, probably floating-rate Treasuries, and it blurs what I would actually hold.
screens.why6: Five sentences in one go is a lot to hear once, the second sentence is a mouthful, and '4.5% to 5%' says acceptably but adds a number to hold.
screens.instead: Imagine Palus. You link your bank, and it puts the reserve you won't touch for months into floating-rate Treasuries, held in your company's name by a regulated custodian. Cash comes back to checking in one to two business days. The people building it believe it would earn 4.5 to 5 percent.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card, asking whether a two-day wait to pull money out would have worked for us is the obvious first check on whether I could use it at all.
screens.why2: "Your last cash decision" is vague to me, since it could be paying a vendor or moving the raise into treasuries; I'd say "the last time you moved or pulled money from where the raise sits."
screens.why3: I know when we last needed to pull cash and whether two days' notice would have been fine, because I run that every week.
screens.why4: The question is about one occasion, so "Only sometimes" doesn't fit, and "Yes, mostly" against "Only sometimes" is a fuzzy split; "Yes, but I'd have had to plan ahead" is the real middle answer.
screens.why5: It keeps the two-day access trade-off without leaking the product's workings, and the Palus name sits on the idea card where it belongs.
screens.why6: It is short, a single question with four short options and one escape, and easy to hold when heard once.
screens.instead: Think of the last time you pulled money from where your raise sits. Would a two-day wait have been fine? Yes, easily; Yes, with some planning ahead; No, we needed it the same day; or I can't tell.

screens.why1: Right after the card and the two-day-wait question, asking whether Palus would have beaten what I actually did with our cash is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: The words are plain, but 'made things better' doesn't say better at what, and for me yield and operational burden pull opposite ways, so I'd have to pick a reading before answering.
screens.why3: I know exactly where our raise sat and why, but whether Palus would have beaten it means guessing at its yield, its sweep and its paperwork against the setup we already run at about 3.2%.
screens.why4: Better, no difference and worse cover it without overlap, and 'I can't tell' is the honest escape for an idea I've only read three lines about.
screens.why5: Palus is the card shown on purpose so nothing leaks, but 'things' blurs whatever advantage the founder meant me to weigh, whether yield, safety or less work.
screens.why6: One short question with three short options and one escape is easy to hold when heard once.
screens.instead: Compared with where your cash sat at your last decision, would Palus have been better for you, or not? It would have been better; No difference; It would have been worse; or I can't tell.

screens.why1: I just said Palus wouldn't have changed much, so asking what would have is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: 'It' and the clipped 'What would have?' make me stop to work out that it means Palus and 'made things better for our cash'; I'd follow it, but on a second pass.
screens.why3: I know exactly what would matter to us: nothing that adds operational burden, since we're happy leaving cash at about 3.2% where it sits.
screens.why4: A box to type in, with no options or chips.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's follow-up on my own answer and adds no product terms beyond the Palus name I was already shown.
screens.why6: It's short and one question, but heard once, 'it' and the trailing 'What would have?' leave me holding the referent from the last question.
screens.instead: You said Palus wouldn't have made much difference. What would have made your cash decision better, if anything?

screens.why1: After asking whether Palus would have helped, it makes sense to ask whether I'd actually move the reserve to get it, since that switch is the whole cost to me.
screens.why2: 'Long-term reserve' and 'bank's treasury' are how I talk about the cash we park in Mercury Treasury, so I get it on first read.
screens.why3: I decide where our reserve sits, so I know my answer: the operational burden of moving it outweighs a bit more yield.
screens.why4: 'Yes' and 'Yes, if it was clearly worth it' overlap, and there is no option for moving only part of the reserve, which is what I'd realistically consider.
screens.why5: It only names Palus from the card and puts the switch in plain banking terms, with nothing of the founder's internal language coming through.
screens.why6: One short sentence and one balanced question, with four brief options and one escape that are easy to hold when heard once.
screens.instead: Palus means moving your reserve out of your bank's treasury. Would you do that, or not? Yes, all of it; Only part of it; Only if the yield gap was big; No. Or say I can't tell.

screens.why1: Right after I said moving our long-term reserve out of the bank's treasury was too much, asking why is the obvious next thing to ask.
screens.why2: Short and plain, but 'that' and 'too much' lean on an answer wording I only half remember, so heard aloud I'd pause a beat to place what 'that' is.
screens.why3: Yes: it's the operational burden, the extra accounts, approvals and audit trail, which matter more to us than a bit more yield over our 3.2%.
screens.why4: A box to type in, no options shown.
screens.why5: It only asks my reason in my terms, with no new product talk or founder wording leaking in.
screens.why6: Five words and one question, easy to hear once and answer, though the bare 'that' relies on the screen before.
screens.instead: What makes moving your reserve out of your bank too much trouble?
